draft.title: WorkSafe insurance
card: In Victoria, an employer must hold WorkSafe insurance. It is also called workers' compensation insurance.
It covers employees who are injured or become ill because of their work. This includes the cost of medical treatment and some of the wages the worker loses while recovering.
The employer pays a premium, which is the regular cost of the insurance. The injured worker does not pay for it.
The duty comes from the law. An employer cannot choose to go without it, even if the work seems low risk, such as office work.
draft.remember: If a Victorian employer has staff, the law requires WorkSafe insurance to cover work injuries.

a.q: Why does a Victorian employer hold WorkSafe insurance?
opts: The law requires it to cover staff injured at work
It covers the owner's losses if customers stop buying
It covers damage to the business's stock and equipment
It is optional, but it lowers the tax the business pays
a.why: WorkSafe insurance is a legal duty for employers, and it covers staff who are injured or become ill because of work. It does not cover business losses or stock, and it is not an optional way to cut tax.
a.clue: Think about who the insurance protects and whether the employer has a choice.

b.q: Priya opens a bakery in Ballarat and hires two part-time workers. One later burns her hand on an oven at work. Who should meet the cost of her medical treatment?
opts: Priya's WorkSafe insurance, paid for by Priya as employer
The injured worker, from her own wages
The ACCC, because it enforces laws on businesses
The customers, through a charge added to prices
b.why: Priya is an employer, so she must hold WorkSafe insurance. It covers staff injured at work, such as the worker burnt at the oven. The worker does not pay for this cover, because the employer pays the premium.
b.clue: Who must hold the insurance, and who pays the premium?

a.best: The law requires it to cover staff injured at work

b.best: Priya's WorkSafe insurance, paid for by Priya as employer

problems.detail: The card says every Victorian employer must hold WorkSafe (WorkCover) insurance and cannot go without it. In fact, an employer only has to register if it pays more than $7,500 a year in rateable wages, or employs apprentices or trainees. The remember line ('If a Victorian employer has staff, the law requires...') repeats this absolute claim. A brief qualifier such as 'most employers' or 'once wages pass a small threshold' would fix it.

check.summary: Both questions are sound and each has one clear right answer. The card and remember line overstate the duty: Victorian employers paying $7,500 or less a year in wages (with no apprentices or trainees) do not have to hold WorkSafe insurance.

proposal.title: WorkSafe insurance
card: In Victoria, most employers must hold WorkSafe insurance, also called workers' compensation insurance. The duty applies once yearly wages pass a small threshold, or if the business employs apprentices or trainees.
It covers employees who are injured or become ill because of their work. This includes the cost of medical treatment and some of the wages the worker loses while recovering.
The employer pays a premium, which is the regular cost of the insurance. The injured worker does not pay for it.
The duty comes from the law. An employer it applies to cannot choose to go without it, even if the work seems low risk, such as office work.
proposal.remember: Past the wages threshold, WorkSafe cover is a legal duty, paid by the employer, that protects injured staff.
